segments.voice: Yesterday in the Devi Mahatmya, Mahisha changed shape again and again, until the goddess pinned him and he had to show himself. Did you stop for one slow drink in the middle of a busy stretch? Day one thousand sixty-six.

Here's a question the gods themselves ask. If the goddess could end Mahisha with a single look, why fight at all? In the fourth chapter the battle is over. The buffalo is dead. The gods, with Indra at their head, bow down with their necks bent and their bodies thrilled, and they praise her. And partway through their hymn, they stop and wonder out loud: you could have burned him to ash just by looking at him. Why didn't you? It's a strange question to ask in a victory song. Their own answer is stranger. Today, the gods' hymn, and the promise the goddess leaves behind before she disappears.
screen: `THE BATTLE IS OVER.` → `WHY NOT ONE LOOK?` → `A HYMN, AND A PROMISE.`

segments.voice: The hymn begins wide. In paraphrase, the gods bow to the goddess who spread out this whole world by her own power, whom even Vishnu and Shiva and Brahma can't fully describe. Then it comes down into ordinary houses. She is good fortune herself in the homes of those who do good, and misfortune in the homes of those who do harm. She is understanding in the hearts of the learned, faith in the good, and modesty in people of noble birth. In this hymn the goddess isn't only on a battlefield. She's at the kitchen table, in what a house becomes. Then the question. Why fight? Why not one look? And the gods answer it themselves. In paraphrase: it's so that the demons, purified by your weapons, might reach the higher worlds. Even toward enemies, your thought is kind. They go further: these demons did enough harm to deserve a long time in hell, and you killed them in battle so that they might reach heaven instead. In the gods' own hymn, the sword is a kind of mercy. Then the goddess speaks. She tells the gods to choose a boon. They say, in paraphrase: our enemy is dead, so everything is done. But if we ever remember you again, come and end our worst troubles. And whoever praises you with this hymn, may they prosper. The goddess agrees, and vanishes. Hold on to that promise. Remembered in trouble, she will come. The next chapter opens with new demons, and the gods, cornered again, remembering exactly this.
screen: `FORTUNE IN THE HOMES OF THE GOOD.` · `WHY NOT BURN HIM WITH A LOOK?` · `EVEN TOWARD ENEMIES, KIND.` · `REMEMBER ME, AND I WILL COME.` · then, large: `THE SWORD AS A KIND OF MERCY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: one kind thought toward a hard person. Settle, and let the breath slow. Bring to mind someone who has made life harder for you, not the hardest, just someone. Notice what rises: tightness, a story, an old argument. Breathe with it. Then, without excusing anything they did, let one small wish form for their good: that they find some peace, or some better way. Let it be small. You don't have to mean it completely. If you pray, you can hold them before God or the goddess in the words you already use. If you don't, let the wish ride out on the breath. The bell holds the time.
The Devi Mahatmya. Today, the gods' hymn after the battle: fortune in good homes, kindness even toward enemies, and a promise to come when remembered.
Your line: the Devi Mahatmya, read whole. Today, when someone hard crosses your mind, send one small good wish their way before you let them go. Day one thousand sixty-six.

howItsDone: The gods' hymn in the fourth chapter of the Devi Mahatmya, sometimes called the Shakradi Stuti after Indra (Shakra), is recited as part of the whole text and is also chanted on its own by some devotees of the goddess.

in the hearts of the learned

myth: the gods' hymn praises the goddess only as a warrior
it also names her as fortune in good homes, understanding, faith and modesty.
the gods ask why she didn't burn Mahisha with a look
and answer it themselves: so that, purified by her weapons, even enemies might reach the higher worlds.
after the hymn, the goddess stays with the gods
she grants their boon and vanishes.

fork.setup: you're the gods. the goddess has killed your enemy and offers you a boon. what do you ask for?
options: that she stay and rule heaven.
that she come and end our troubles whenever we remember her.
fork.reveal: they say everything is done, then ask: when we remember you again, come and end our worst troubles. she agrees, and vanishes.

original.note: Sanskrit: stuti, a hymn of praise. The fourth chapter is the gods' stuti to the goddess.

trapdoor: what you thought: a victory song after a battle.
what it means: the gods praise her in battle and in ordinary homes, call her sword a kindness even to enemies, and win her promise to return.
what a scholar hears: chapter 4, the Shakradi Stuti, ending with the boon that the next chapter's gods remember when Shumbha and Nishumbha rise.

sources.ref: Devi Mahatmya, chapter 4 (the gods' hymn and the boon)

notes: Chapter 4 paraphrased: the gods led by Indra (Śakra) praise the goddess; she is fortune (śrī) in the dwellings of the virtuous and misfortune (alakṣmī) in those of the wicked, intelligence in the hearts of the learned, faith in the good, modesty in the high-born; why not reduce the demon to ashes by sight? so that, purified by her weapons, they may reach higher worlds; her mind is kind even to enemies; they had done enough evil to stay long in hell, but dying in battle they reach heaven. Confirm wording and that 'reach heaven' is fair.
The boon: whenever remembered again she will destroy the gods' worst calamities, and those who praise her with these hymns will prosper. Confirm.

'The sword as a kind of mercy' and the practice of wishing good to a hard person are drawn from the hymn's own reading of her kindness to enemies; confirm a Keeper is comfortable with the practice's framing.
'Shakradi Stuti' named only in howItsDone; confirm the name.
Editor pass: review question now matches 1065's revised carry (a slow drink mid-stretch); 'the goddess isn't only on a battlefield' is now attributed to the hymn.
